title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about the critical skills in action. You already know what being critical means and that it is a mindset. Here you put three of its core moves to work: analysis (breaking a source into its parts), evaluation (weighing an interpretation against alternatives), and synthesis (drawing several sources into an argument of your own).

These are the skills university assignments ask for by name. When a brief says analyse, evaluate or discuss, it is naming one of these moves. Being able to perform them, not just recognise them, is what moves your work from reporting what sources say to building a case of your own.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: analyse an academic source by separating its claim, evidence and reasoning
evaluate an interpretation by weighing its relative value against alternatives
synthesise several sources into an argument of your own.

title: In real academic practice
body: Analysis, evaluation and synthesis are the engine of academic work. Every essay that asks you to evaluate a theory, every literature review that draws sources together, every seminar where interpretations are weighed, runs on these three skills. Building them now carries into every module of your degree, and into the reasoned judgement that professional work later asks of you.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons, one for each skill. First, analysis: taking a source apart to see its claim, evidence and reasoning. Second, evaluation: weighing an interpretation against alternatives. Third, synthesis: drawing several sources into an argument of your own. Work through them in order; each skill builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_items.text: I can analyse an academic source by separating its claim, evidence and reasoning.
I can evaluate an interpretation by weighing its relative value against alternatives.
I can synthesise several sources into an argument of my own.

title: Orientation
body: You already know that being critical is a mindset, and what active engagement with a source looks like. This lesson turns the mindset into a skill you perform. Analysis is the first of three: taking a source apart to see what it is actually claiming, on what evidence, and by what reasoning.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to do more than recognise analysis when you see it. The aim is to perform it on a real academic source: to separate a claim from its evidence and its reasoning yourself, rather than taking the source's conclusion whole.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: analyse a source by separating its claim, the evidence behind it and the reasoning that links them
compare an analytical reading of a journal article with a passive one
apply analysis to a source in {{context}}, separating its claim, evidence and reasoning

title: Concept: definition
body:
Analysis means breaking an interpretation, a body of evidence or a data set down into its parts through close examination. To analyse a source is not to summarise what it says but to open it up: to separate the claim it makes from the evidence it rests on and the reasoning that links the two.

This matters because analysis is the first of the critical skills. You cannot weigh a source fairly, or combine it with others, until you have seen its parts clearly. Taking an interpretation apart is what lets everything else, evaluation and synthesis, begin.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a source you read recently for your course. If you had to separate its central claim from the evidence behind it, could you? What was it actually arguing?

title: Summary
body: Analysis means breaking a source into its parts, its claim, the evidence behind it, and the reasoning that links them, through close examination rather than summary. You can now explain what analysis is and recognise it in how a student reads a journal article. The next lesson builds on it: once a source is taken apart, evaluation weighs how good its parts are against the alternatives.

_items.title: See pages 119 to 123 of Chapter 8, 'Critical thought and developing a critical edge in writing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you took a source apart. This lesson asks the next question: how good is it? Evaluation weighs an interpretation, judging its value not in isolation but against the alternatives, and always with reasons.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to form a judgement and defend it, not just to notice that evaluation is happening. The aim is to weigh one interpretation against another yourself and say, with reasons, which better accounts for the evidence.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: compare an interpretation with its alternatives on how well each fits the evidence
analyse what a full evaluation adds beyond taking an interpretation apart
apply evaluation to a source in {{context}}, weighing it against alternatives

title: Concept: definition
body:
Evaluation means assessing the relative value, the importance or significance, of one factor or interpretation against that of others. You do not evaluate a source in isolation: you weigh it against alternatives, asking which better accounts for the evidence, and you give reasons for your verdict.

This matters because evaluation is where criticism earns its name. Analysis shows you the parts of a source; evaluation judges how strong they are and how they compare with rival readings. A judgement without reasons is only a preference. Evaluation is a reasoned verdict about relative worth.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of two explanations you have met for the same thing in your subject. Which did you find more convincing, and could you say why, in terms of the evidence rather than preference?

title: Summary
body: Evaluation means weighing the relative value of an interpretation against alternatives, with reasons, rather than judging it in isolation. You can now tell evaluation apart from analysis and choose an evaluative question to ask of a source. The next lesson completes the set: synthesis draws several evaluated sources together into an argument of your own.

_items.title: See pages 117 to 121 of Chapter 8, 'Critical thought and developing a critical edge in writing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: You have taken a source apart and weighed it against others. This lesson is about building something from them. Synthesis draws several sources together into an argument of your own, one that none of them stated alone.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to build, not just combine. The aim is to make several sources speak to each other, set agreement against disagreement, and form from the tension a claim of your own, expressed in your discipline's own vocabulary.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: compare synthesis with summarising sources one at a time
analyse what makes a piece of writing synthesis rather than a run of summaries
apply synthesis to sources in {{context}}, drawing them into an argument of your own

title: Concept: definition
body:
Synthesis means drawing together different interpretations or evidence in forming and expressing an argument of your own. It is not a list of summaries set side by side: it makes sources speak to each other, noting where they agree and conflict, and builds from them a position none of them stated alone.

This matters because synthesis is where your own voice enters. Analysis and evaluation work on sources one at a time; synthesis uses them together, as evidence and foils for a claim of your own. It is also expressed in your discipline's own vocabulary, the terms that carry meaning within its discourse, so that the argument reads as one your field will recognise.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of an essay where you used several sources. Did they speak to each other, or sit in separate paragraphs? What claim of your own could have drawn them together?

title: Summary
body: Synthesis means drawing several sources together into an argument of your own, making them speak to each other rather than summarising each in turn, and expressing the result in your discipline's own vocabulary. You can now tell synthesis apart from summary and identify a synthesis move across sources. With analysis, evaluation and synthesis in hand, you can put the critical skills to work on purpose.

_items.title: See pages 128 to 133 of Chapter 8, 'Critical thought and developing a critical edge in writing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. The critical skills are no longer just words: they are moves you can make. You can analyse a source by separating its claim, evidence and reasoning; you can evaluate an interpretation by weighing its relative value against alternatives, with reasons; and you can synthesise several sources into an argument of your own. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, analysis, evaluation and synthesis are what you practise in every module. Each time a brief says analyse or evaluate, each literature review that draws sources together, each argument you build rather than report, is these skills at work. They are also what research and professional practice reward: the ability to take evidence apart, weigh it, and build a reasoned case travels well beyond your degree.

title: Where this goes next
body: One direction goes deeper and others go wider. Going deeper: the advanced criticality course takes these skills into articulating criticality in your own voice, across whole pieces of writing. Going wider: analysis, evaluation and synthesis underpin Academic Writing, Researching and Research Methods, and Reflective Practice, where you put them to work on real tasks. If the mindset behind these skills feels shaky, the introductory criticality course is where it is built.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The parts of an interpretation
body: Four facets of what analysis asks you to do. Turn each card to see the move.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over. Work through all four.

back.body: Analysis is not retelling what a source says. It means opening it up: separating the claim it makes from the evidence it offers and the reasoning that links them, so you can see how the parts fit together.

To analyse is to look closely at the parts of an interpretation: which claim is central, what evidence each part rests on, and what is assumed but never argued. You read for structure, not only for the conclusion.
Most academic interpretations share the same parts: a claim, the evidence behind it, and the reasoning that connects them. Naming these three parts in a source is the first move of analysis.
You cannot weigh a source (evaluation) or combine it with others (synthesis) until you have taken it apart. Analysis is the skill the other two are built on.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Consider two students using the same journal article in an essay.

{{learner-a}} reads the article and takes its conclusion as the point: the author argues that the effect is real, so {{learner-a}} notes that down and quotes it. The article has been read and used, but it has been treated as one undivided statement. {{learner-a}} has not asked what the central claim actually is, what evidence sits behind it, or how the author reasons from one to the other. This is reading without analysis.

{{learner-b}} reads the same article and takes it apart. The central claim is this; the evidence offered for it is that study and that dataset; the reasoning runs from the evidence to the claim in these steps, and one step is assumed rather than argued. {{learner-b}} now sees the article as a structure of parts, not a single verdict. This is analysis.

Both students read the same article. Only {{learner-b}} separated its claim, evidence and reasoning, which is what makes a reading analytical.

title: Analysis moves
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These moves turn analysis into something you do. Try them on your next source.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I stated the source's central claim in my own words?
Have I separated the evidence from the claim it is meant to support?
Have I traced the reasoning that links the evidence to the claim?
Have I noticed anything the source assumes without arguing?
Have I looked at the structure of the article, its sections, not only its conclusion?
Have I resisted simply summarising what the source says?

title: Formative check: what analysis means
displayTitle: Which of these is analysing a source, rather than summarising or judging it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option is analysing the source?

_items.text: Breaking it into its parts - claim, evidence and reasoning - through close examination.
_items.feedback: Yes. Analysis separates a source into its parts to see how it is built.

_items.text: Summarising accurately what the source says.
_items.feedback: An accurate summary reports the source; it does not take it apart.

_items.text: Finding fault with the source and listing its weaknesses.
_items.feedback: Fault-finding is not analysis; analysis opens a source up rather than attacking it.

_items.text: Collecting as many sources on the topic as you can.
_items.feedback: Quantity of sources is not analysis; analysis works closely on one source's parts.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Analysis means breaking a source into its claim, evidence and reasoning through close examination.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about separating a source into its parts, rather than summarising or judging it.
_incorrect.final: Analysis means breaking a source into its parts - claim, evidence and reasoning. Summarising reports it, fault-finding attacks it, and collecting sources does neither.

title: Formative check: recognising analysis
displayTitle: Comparing the two readings in the worked example, what did the analytical one do that the passive one did not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the analytical reading do that the passive one did not?

_items.text: They separated the article into its claim, the evidence for it, and the reasoning linking them.
_items.feedback: Yes. Taking the article apart into its parts is analysis.

_items.text: They quoted the article's conclusion as evidence for their point.
_items.feedback: Both students used the article; quoting the conclusion is not analysis.

_items.text: They read the article more carefully the second time.
_items.feedback: Care alone is not analysis; separating the parts is.

_items.text: They accepted the author's conclusion because it was published.
_items.feedback: Accepting a conclusion whole is exactly what analysis does not do.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student took the article apart into claim, evidence and reasoning, which is analysis.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student DID with the article, beyond reading or quoting it.
_incorrect.final: The second student was analytical because they separated the article's claim, evidence and reasoning. Quoting, re-reading or accepting the conclusion are not analysis.

title: Formative check: analysing a source
displayTitle: You are analysing a key source in {{context}}. Which approach actually takes it apart, rather than citing, weighing or combining it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which approach takes the source apart?

_items.text: Separating the source's central claim, its evidence, and the reasoning that links them.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is analysis in {{context}}: taking the source apart into its parts.

_items.text: Noting the source's conclusion so you can cite it later.
_items.feedback: Noting the conclusion keeps the source whole; it does not analyse it.

_items.text: Deciding whether the source is better than a rival reading.
_items.feedback: Weighing one reading against another is evaluation, which comes after analysis.

_items.text: Drawing the source together with others into an argument of your own.
_items.feedback: Combining sources is synthesis, not analysis.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, analysis means separating a source's claim, evidence and reasoning.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that takes the source APART, rather than citing, weighing or combining it.
_incorrect.final: Analysis in {{context}} means separating a source's claim, evidence and reasoning. Citing it leaves it whole, weighing it is evaluation, and combining sources is synthesis.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: What evaluation asks
body: Four facets of what it means to evaluate an interpretation. Open each to see the move.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Weighing, not describing
_items.body: Evaluation asks how much a claim or interpretation is worth: how strong it is, how well supported, how significant. It goes beyond saying what a source claims to judging how far it holds.

_items.title: Relative value
_items.body: You evaluate by comparison. A factor's value is not absolute; it is weighed against alternatives. Asking 'compared with what?' is the heart of evaluation.

_items.title: With reasons
_items.body: To evaluate is to give grounds: this interpretation is stronger because its evidence is wider, or weaker because its sample is narrow. A verdict without reasons is a preference, not an evaluation.

_items.title: Built on analysis
_items.body: You can only weigh a source once you have taken it apart. Evaluation uses the parts analysis found - claim, evidence, reasoning - and asks how good each is and how it compares with rival interpretations.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students write about the same interpretation of a well-known finding.

{{learner-a}} takes the interpretation apart neatly: here is the claim, here is the evidence offered for it, here is the reasoning. The account is accurate, and it stops there. {{learner-a}} has analysed the interpretation but not weighed it: there is no sense of how strong it is, or how it stands against any other reading of the same evidence. This is analysis without evaluation.

{{learner-b}} goes further. Having seen the parts, {{learner-b}} sets this interpretation against a rival one and asks which better accounts for the evidence. The first explains more of the data but rests on a narrow sample; the second is wider but vaguer. {{learner-b}} judges the first stronger on balance, and says why. This is evaluation.

Both students understood the interpretation. Only {{learner-b}} weighed its relative value against an alternative, with reasons, which is what evaluation adds to analysis.

title: Evaluation moves
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These moves turn evaluation into something you do. Try them on your next source.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I asked how strong the source's evidence actually is?
Have I compared this interpretation with at least one alternative?
Have I asked which interpretation better accounts for the evidence?
Have I given reasons for my verdict, not just a preference?
Have I weighed significance, not only accuracy?
Have I resisted treating one source as the only possible reading?

title: Formative check: what evaluation means
displayTitle: Which of these is evaluating an interpretation, rather than analysing, synthesising or restating it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option is evaluating the interpretation?

_items.text: Weighing its relative value against alternatives, with reasons.
_items.feedback: Yes. Evaluation weighs an interpretation against others and gives reasons.

_items.text: Breaking it into its claim, evidence and reasoning.
_items.feedback: That is analysis, which comes before evaluation.

_items.text: Drawing it together with other sources into your own argument.
_items.feedback: That is synthesis, not evaluation.

_items.text: Restating what the interpretation says in your own words.
_items.feedback: Restating is description; evaluation judges value with reasons.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Evaluation means weighing an interpretation's relative value against alternatives, with reasons.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about weighing value against alternatives, rather than taking apart, combining or restating.
_incorrect.final: Evaluation weighs an interpretation's relative value against alternatives, with reasons. Breaking down is analysis, combining is synthesis, and restating is description.

title: Formative check: evaluation versus analysis
displayTitle: Analysing the worked example, what did the second student add that the first did not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second student add that the first did not?

_items.text: Weighed the interpretation against a rival and judged which better fit the evidence, with reasons.
_items.feedback: Yes. Weighing against an alternative, with reasons, is evaluation.

_items.text: Separated the interpretation into its claim, evidence and reasoning.
_items.feedback: Both students did that; it is analysis, which the first student also did.

_items.text: Summarised the interpretation more accurately.
_items.feedback: Accurate summary is not what the second student added; weighing is.

_items.text: Quoted the original source more fully.
_items.feedback: Fuller quotation is not evaluation; weighing value against alternatives is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student weighed the interpretation against a rival, with reasons, which is evaluation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The first student already took the interpretation apart. Look for what the second student ADDED.
_incorrect.final: The second student evaluated: weighing the interpretation against an alternative and judging which better fit the evidence, with reasons. Both had already analysed it.

title: Formative check: an evaluative question
displayTitle: You are evaluating a source in {{context}}. Which question actually weighs it against alternatives, rather than taking it apart or combining it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which question weighs the source against alternatives?

_items.text: How does this interpretation compare with alternatives, and which better fits the evidence?
_items.feedback: Yes. Comparing value against alternatives is the evaluative move in {{context}}.

_items.text: What is the source's central claim, and what evidence sits behind it?
_items.feedback: That is an analytical question; it takes the source apart rather than weighing it.

_items.text: How can I combine this source with two others into my own argument?
_items.feedback: That is a synthesis question, not an evaluative one.

_items.text: How can I restate the source's conclusion in my own words?
_items.feedback: That is description; it does not weigh the source's value.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, the evaluative question compares an interpretation's value against alternatives.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the question that WEIGHS the source against alternatives, rather than taking it apart or combining it.
_incorrect.final: The evaluative question in {{context}} compares an interpretation with alternatives and asks which fits the evidence better. The others analyse, synthesise or describe.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: What synthesis asks
body: Four facets of what it means to synthesise sources. Select each tab to see the move.
instruction: Select each tab to read about that facet.

_items.title: Drawing together
_items.body: Synthesis means combining several sources into something none of them said alone: a position of your own, built from, but not reducible to, what you read.

_items.title: Not a list of summaries
_items.body: Summarising sources one after another is not synthesis. Synthesis makes them speak to each other: where they agree, where they conflict, and what follows for your argument.

_items.title: In service of your argument
_items.body: Synthesis is always directed. You draw sources together to build and express a claim of your own, using them as evidence and foils rather than as the point itself.

_items.title: The language of your discipline
_items.body: Synthesis is expressed in your subject's own vocabulary, the terms that carry meaning within its discourse. Using them accurately is part of drawing sources into an argument your field will recognise.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students bring the same three sources to an essay.

{{learner-a}} writes a paragraph on each source in turn: the first found this, the second argued that, the third reported something else. Each summary is accurate, and the three never meet. No claim of {{learner-a}}'s own emerges; the reader is left with three reports side by side. This is summary, not synthesis.

{{learner-b}} makes the three sources speak to each other. Two broadly agree, while the third dissents on one point; {{learner-b}} sets the agreement against the dissent and argues, from the tension between them, a position none of the three stated alone. The sources become evidence for {{learner-b}}'s own claim. This is synthesis.

Both students used the same three sources. Only {{learner-b}} drew them together into an argument of their own, which is what makes writing synthesis rather than summary.

title: Synthesis moves
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These moves turn synthesis into something you do. Try them across your next set of sources.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I identified where my sources agree and where they conflict?
Have I made the sources speak to each other, rather than listing them one at a time?
Have I built a claim of my own that none of the sources stated alone?
Am I using the sources as evidence for my argument, not as the argument itself?
Have I used my discipline's own vocabulary accurately?
Have I resisted summarising each source separately?

title: Formative check: what synthesis means
displayTitle: Which of these is synthesis, rather than summarising, evaluating or analysing sources?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option is synthesis?

_items.text: Drawing several sources together into an argument of your own.
_items.feedback: Yes. Synthesis combines sources into a claim none stated alone.

_items.text: Summarising each source accurately, one after another.
_items.feedback: A row of summaries is not synthesis; synthesis makes sources speak to each other.

_items.text: Weighing one interpretation's value against another.
_items.feedback: That is evaluation, not synthesis.

_items.text: Breaking a single source into its claim and evidence.
_items.feedback: That is analysis, which works on one source at a time.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Synthesis draws several sources together into an argument of your own.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about combining sources into your own claim, rather than summarising, weighing or taking apart.
_incorrect.final: Synthesis draws several sources together into an argument of your own. Summarising lists them, evaluation weighs one against another, and analysis breaks a single source down.

title: Formative check: synthesis versus summary
displayTitle: Analysing the worked example, what made the second student's writing synthesis rather than summary?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's writing synthesis rather than summary?

_items.text: They set the sources against each other and built a claim of their own that none stated alone.
_items.feedback: Yes. Making sources speak to each other to build your own claim is synthesis.

_items.text: They wrote a separate, accurate paragraph on each source.
_items.feedback: Separate paragraphs are summary, which is what the first student did.

_items.text: They used more sources than the first student.
_items.feedback: Both used the same three sources; number is not the point.

_items.text: They quoted each source more fully.
_items.feedback: Fuller quotation is still summary if the sources never meet.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student made the sources speak to each other and built a claim of their own, which is synthesis.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student did ACROSS the sources, rather than reporting each one.
_incorrect.final: The second student synthesised: setting the sources against each other and building a claim none stated alone. Separate paragraphs, more sources or fuller quotes are still summary.

title: Formative check: a synthesis move
displayTitle: You are working with several sources in {{context}}. Which move actually draws them into an argument of your own, rather than summarising, weighing or taking one apart?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move draws the sources into an argument of your own?

_items.text: Drawing the sources together into a claim of your own that none stated alone.
_items.feedback: Yes. Building your own claim from several sources is synthesis in {{context}}.

_items.text: Summarising each source in a paragraph of its own.
_items.feedback: Separate summaries do not synthesise; the sources never meet.

_items.text: Weighing which single source is the strongest.
_items.feedback: That is evaluation, not synthesis.

_items.text: Separating one source into its claim and evidence.
_items.feedback: That is analysis, which works on one source at a time.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, synthesis draws several sources into a claim of your own.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that BUILDS your own claim from several sources, rather than summarising, weighing or taking one apart.
_incorrect.final: Synthesis in {{context}} draws several sources together into a claim of your own. Summarising lists them, evaluation weighs them, and analysis breaks one down.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: analysis, taking a source apart; evaluation, weighing it against alternatives; and synthesis, drawing several sources into an argument of your own. On their own they are three separate skills. This lesson brings them together into one critical practice.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are not learning three new skills. The aim is to see analysis, evaluation and synthesis as one connected practice rather than three separate exercises, so that it carries on past this course and into the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect analysis, evaluation and synthesis as one critical practice rather than three separate moves
analyse how the three skills work together in a student's handling of sources
apply the three skills together to sources in your {{context}} study

title: Concept: definition
body: Working critically with sources is one practice, not three. You take a source apart to see its claim, evidence and reasoning; you weigh its parts against other readings; and you draw several sources together into an argument of your own. Analysis, evaluation and synthesis are the parts of that one practice, each building on the one before.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, you rarely use one skill on its own. Reading for an essay, you take each source apart, weigh the interpretations against each other, and draw them into a claim of your own. The three skills run together, one leading into the next, whenever you build an argument from what you read.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a piece of writing coming up in your course that draws on several sources. How would you take those sources apart, weigh them, and draw them into an argument of your own?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Analysis, evaluation and synthesis are most useful when you run them together. You take a source apart, weigh it against others, and draw several into an argument of your own. It is the three skills working as one practice, not any single move, that turns reading into a case of your own.

title: The steps as one process
displayTitle: The steps as one process
body: Working critically with sources is one practice that builds up step by step, each move resting on the one before. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Analyse
_items.body: Take each source apart to see its claim, the evidence behind it and the reasoning that links them.

_items.title: Evaluate
_items.body: Weigh each interpretation against the alternatives, and say which one better accounts for the evidence.

_items.title: Synthesise
_items.body: Draw the sources together, setting agreement against disagreement, to build a claim of your own.

_items.title: Articulate
_items.body: Express that claim in your discipline's own vocabulary, so your field recognises the argument.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students write an essay from the same three sources. One takes each source apart but stops there, listing what each says in turn. The other takes them apart, weighs the readings against one another, then draws them into a claim of their own. The second essay argues a position of its own, where the first only reports, and using the three skills together is what made the difference.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to work critically with sources
body: Use these to keep analysis, evaluation and synthesis working together, rather than treating each as a separate task.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I take the source apart, separating its claim, evidence and reasoning?
Did I weigh the interpretation against alternatives, with reasons, rather than judging it alone?
Did I let the three skills build on one another, not stop at taking the source apart?
Did I make my sources speak to each other, rather than summarising each in turn?
Did I build a claim of my own and express it in my subject's own words?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat analysis, evaluation and synthesis as one connected practice rather than three separate exercises?
body: Why is it more useful to treat analysis, evaluation and synthesis as one connected practice rather than three separate exercises?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat analysis, evaluation and synthesis as one connected practice rather than three separate exercises?

_items.text: Because each skill builds on the one before: analysis gives you the parts to weigh, evaluation tells you which are strong, and synthesis draws them into your own argument.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three skills feed one another, so working them together is what builds a reasoned argument from sources.

_items.text: Because doing all three at once takes less thought than doing them one at a time.
_items.feedback: It is not about less effort. Each skill still asks something distinct; the point is that they work together.

_items.text: Because analysis on its own is enough to build an argument from sources.
_items.feedback: Analysis only gives you the parts. You still need to weigh them and draw them together.

_items.text: Because it means you never have to judge which interpretation is stronger.
_items.feedback: Judging which interpretation is stronger is evaluation, and it is part of the practice, not something you skip.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three skills feed one another, so working them together is what turns sources into an argument of your own.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how each skill depends on the one before it.

displayTitle: A student takes an article apart into its claim and evidence, weighs it against a rival reading, then draws both into a claim of their own. What does this show?
body: A student takes an article apart into its claim and evidence, weighs it against a rival reading, then draws both into a claim of their own. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student takes an article apart into its claim and evidence, weighs it against a rival reading, then draws both into a claim of their own. What does this show?

_items.text: The three critical skills working as one practice: analysis, then evaluation, then synthesis, each feeding the next.
_items.feedback: Yes. The student moved from taking the source apart, to weighing it, to building an argument.

_items.text: Only analysis, because the student began by taking the article apart.
_items.feedback: Analysis was the first move, but the student also weighed the reading and built a claim.

_items.text: Only summary, because the student used more than one source.
_items.feedback: Using sources together to build a claim is synthesis, not summary.

_items.text: Evaluation on its own, because the student compared two readings.
_items.feedback: Weighing the readings was evaluation, but it sat inside the fuller practice of all three skills.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Analysis, evaluation and synthesis ran together as one practice, each building on the one before.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at the three moves the student made, in order.

displayTitle: You want to use the three critical skills together to work with sources in {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats them as one practice?
body: You want to use the three critical skills together to work with sources in {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats them as one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use the three critical skills together to work with sources in your subject this term. Which plan best treats them as one practice?

_items.text: For each source, take it apart, weigh it against other readings, then draw several together into a claim of your own.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs all three skills together, from taking a source apart to building an argument.

_items.text: Summarise each source in turn, and stop once you have described them all.
_items.feedback: Summarising each in turn is not synthesis, and it skips weighing them too.

_items.text: Take every source apart in detail, but never weigh one reading against another.
_items.feedback: Analysis without evaluation leaves out a key skill. The three work together.

_items.text: Pick the first interpretation you read and build your whole argument on it alone.
_items.feedback: Building on one reading, unweighed, skips both evaluation and synthesis.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Taking each source apart, weighing it, and drawing sources together keeps the three skills working as one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan uses all three skills, not just one.
